items.title: GDC Tips: Plotting Functions & Analysis Tools

moments.title: Plotting and analysing a function
moments.text: The presenter introduces graphing and the calculator’s graph-analysis tools.

moments.title: A cannonball’s height
moments.text: A height–time graph is used to ask about maximum height, landing time, initial height and when the ball reaches a given height.

moments.title: Enter the quadratic model
moments.text: Enter $h(t)=-2t^2+20t+8$, using the calculator’s graph variable in place of $t$.

moments.title: The first window hides the graph’s features
moments.text: The default view is too narrow to show the maximum and landing point; change the viewing window.

moments.title: Zoom and set useful bounds
moments.text: Zoom out and adjust the horizontal and vertical bounds to display the parabola’s important features.

moments.title: Maximum height
moments.text: The maximum is $(5,58)$: after $5$ seconds the height is $58$ metres.

moments.title: Landing time from a zero
moments.text: Find the positive zero, approximately $10.4$ seconds. The negative zero lies outside the real-world time interval.

moments.title: Initial height
moments.text: The vertical intercept is $(0,8)$, so the ball starts $8$ metres above ground.

moments.title: Intersect with a horizontal line
moments.text: Graph $y=40$ and find the first intersection at $(2,40)$. The second intersection is $(8,40)$, on the way down.

moments.title: Review the features
moments.text: The presenter revisits the maximum, zero, vertical intercept and intersection as answers to questions about the model.

notes.title: Window versus domain
notes.text: A window such as $-5\leq t\leq15$ helps display the full curve. It does not mean negative time or time after the ball lands is physically meaningful.
notes.write: For this model the meaningful interval is approximately $0\leq t\leq10.4$.

notes.title: One height can occur twice
notes.text: The height $40$ m occurs at $t=2$ and $t=8$ seconds. Read the question carefully: the first time is $2$ seconds, while both times answer when the height is $40$ m.

ican.text: I can choose and label axes and a suitable window to sketch a function.
I can identify intercepts, turning points and intersections and interpret their coordinates in context.
I can distinguish a function’s domain from the part displayed in a calculator window.
I can restrict a model to a meaningful domain and check whether graph-based answers make sense.

ku.text: The graph of $y=f(x)$ consists of points $(x,f(x))$ with $x$ in the domain. Label each axis with the quantity and units where relevant.
An $x$-intercept has $y=0$ and solves $f(x)=0$. The $y$-intercept is $(0,f(0))$ only if $0$ is in the domain.
A turning point is where a curve changes from increasing to decreasing or vice versa. Its coordinates give both the input and the output at the maximum or minimum.
Intersections of $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ satisfy $f(x)=g(x)$. A horizontal line $y=k$ can meet a graph more than once, once or not at all.
A sketch should show the correct overall shape and essential features. Label exact values when known and indicate approximations clearly; a sketch need not be drawn to scale.
A viewing window is a display choice. It can hide features or show inputs outside a model’s domain. Adjust bounds and scale, then check conclusions algebraically or numerically.
In a real-world model, exclude inputs and outputs that do not make sense in context, even if the algebraic function is defined there.

misc.weak: The calculator shows no roots, so none exist.
misc.better: Check whether the viewing window includes the relevant intercepts, then use algebra or a solver.

misc.weak: The maximum is $16$ seconds at $3$ metres.
misc.better: Read the ordered pair in axis order: $(3,16)$ means $3$ seconds and $16$ metres.

misc.weak: The graphing window begins at $-2$, so negative time belongs to the model.
misc.better: The window and contextual domain are separate. Restrict time to the interval for which the model describes the situation.

misc.weak: A height is reached only once because the calculator found one intersection.
misc.better: Look for all intersections on the meaningful domain. A ball can pass the same height while rising and falling.

misc.weak: Join every visible part of a graph across a break.
misc.better: Respect restrictions, holes, endpoints and asymptotes. A viewing window does not remove a discontinuity.

terms.text: A point where the graph meets an axis. State its coordinates, not just a number, when asked for the point.
A point at which the graph changes direction locally, from increasing to decreasing or from decreasing to increasing.
The range of inputs and outputs displayed on a graphing screen; it need not equal the domain or range.
A point common to two graphs; its input solves the equation obtained by setting the two outputs equal.

worked.prompt: A ball’s height above the ground is modelled by $h(t)=-t^2+6t+7$ metres, where $t$ is the number of seconds after launch. The model applies until the ball first hits the ground.

parts.label: a
parts.q: Find the initial height and the time when the ball hits the ground. State the meaningful domain.
parts.a: $h(0)=7$, so the initial height is $7$ m. Solve $-t^2+6t+7=0$: $-(t-7)(t+1)=0$, giving $t=7$ or $t=-1$. Negative time is outside the situation, so landing occurs after $7$ s and the domain is $0\leq t\leq7$.

parts.label: b
parts.q: Find and interpret the maximum point.
parts.a: Complete the square: $h(t)=-(t-3)^2+16$. The maximum is $(3,16)$: the ball reaches $16$ m after $3$ s.

parts.label: c
parts.q: Find all times when the ball is $12$ m high.
parts.a: Set $-t^2+6t+7=12$, so $t^2-6t+5=0$ and $(t-1)(t-5)=0$. Both $t=1$ s and $t=5$ s lie in the domain. The ball passes this height on the way up and on the way down.

parts.label: d
parts.q: Describe a labelled sketch of the model.
parts.a: Label the horizontal axis $t$ (seconds) and the vertical axis $h$ (metres). Draw only the downward-opening arc for $0\leq t\leq7$, through $(0,7)$, the maximum $(3,16)$ and $(7,0)$. The line $h=12$ meets it at $(1,12)$ and $(5,12)$.

kq.q: How can a graph help solve $f(x)=k$?
kq.model: Draw $y=f(x)$ and $y=k$, then find all intersection inputs in the relevant domain. Check whether approximate values meet the required accuracy.

kq.q: Why might a calculator show an extra root?
kq.model: It graphs the algebraic expression in the chosen window, which can include values outside the context. Check each root against the model’s meaningful domain.

kq.q: Why is a sketch with a labelled maximum more useful than an unlabelled curve?
kq.model: The shape shows the overall behaviour; the labelled point tells the reader the input where the maximum occurs and its value.
